title: Chapter 56 — Of the Less Erroneous Pictures of Whales, and the True
paragraphs: In connection with the monstrous pictures of whales, I am strongly tempted here to take up those still more monstrous stories about them which are found in certain books, both ancient and modern, especially in Pliny, Purchas, Hakluyt, Harris, Cuvier, and so forth. But I will let that matter pass.

I know of only four published outlines of the great Sperm Whale: Colnett's, Huggins's, Frederick Cuvier's, and Beale's. In the previous chapter Colnett and Cuvier were mentioned. Huggins's is far better than theirs, but by great odds, Beale's is the best. All of Beale's drawings of this whale are good, except the middle figure in his picture of three whales in various positions. His frontispiece, showing boats attacking Sperm Whales, though no doubt designed to be exciting, is rather bad. But his supplementary picture of a Sperm Whale, when compared to any other published version, gives something approaching a faithful likeness.

Of the Right Whale, the best outline pictures are in Scoresby. But they are drawn on too small a scale to make much impression. He has only one picture of whaling scenes, and this is a real deficiency, because it is only through such pictures, when done well, that you can get anything like a truthful idea of the living whale as seen by his living hunters.

But taken all together, by far the finest — though in some details not the most accurate — depictions of whales and whaling scenes to be found anywhere are two large French engravings, well executed, and based on paintings by one Garnery. They represent attacks on the Sperm and Right Whale respectively. In the first engraving a noble Sperm Whale is shown in the full majesty of his power, just risen beneath a boat from the ocean depths, bearing high in the air upon his back the shattered fragments of the boat and the bodies of the crew. On the other side, the harpooner is seen with his weapon aimed, ready for a dart at the beast's throat.

In the second engraving, the boat is in the act of drawing alongside the barnacle-crusted flank of a large running Right Whale, which rolls his black weedy bulk in the sea like some mossy rock-slide from the Patagonian cliffs. His jets are upright, full, and black like soot, so that from such abundant smoke in the chimney, you would think there must be a fine supper cooking in the great bowels below. Sea birds are pecking at the small crabs, shellfish, and other sea delicacies which the Right Whale sometimes carries on his pestilent back. And all the while the thick-lipped leviathan is rushing through the deep, leaving tons of tumbling white curds in his wake.

Who this painter Garnery is, or was, I do not know. But I would stake my life that he was either practically familiar with his subject or else marvelously tutored by some experienced whaleman. The French are the ones for painting action. Go and look at all the paintings of Europe, and where will you find such a gallery of living and breathing commotion on canvas as in that triumphal hall at Versailles, where the viewer fights his way through the consecutive great battles of France? Every major historical engagement is there, with one painting after another.

The natural talent of the French for capturing the picturesque seems particularly evident in their paintings and engravings of whaling scenes. With not one tenth of England's experience in the fishery, and not the thousandth part of America's, they have nevertheless furnished both nations with the only finished sketches capable of conveying the real spirit of the whale hunt. For the most part, the English and American whale artists seem content with presenting the mechanical outline of things — the unvarnished facts. But it is the French who capture the drama.

In addition to those fine engravings by Garnery, there are two other French engravings worthy of note, by someone who signs himself "H. Durand." One of them, though not precisely suited to our present purpose, nevertheless deserves mention on other grounds. It is a quiet noontime scene among the islands of the Pacific: a French whaler anchored inshore in a calm, lazily taking on water. The loosened sails of the ship and the long leaves of the palms in the background both droop together in the breathless air. This painting captures something of the peculiar tranquility of the Pacific.
